title: Steven Pinker is WRONG about the decline of violence
summary: A video essay disputing Steven Pinker's claim that prehistoric people were far more violent, arguing that war arose with farming and settled societies.

assertions.quote: lack of archaeological evidence for warfare suggests that it was rare or absent for most of human pre-history

verdicts.note: Paleolithic evidence of warfare is sparse, but sites like Nataruk and Jebel Sahaba show group killing at or before the dawn of farming, and the record is thin both ways.

assertions.quote: war likely emerged at the end of the ice age with the advent of farming around 10 000 bc

verdicts.note: Signs of warfare rise sharply with settlement and farming in many regions, though some earlier group violence existed.

assertions.quote: surely peace is the norm and violence the exception not the other way around

verdicts.note: Humans show a capacity for both coalitional violence and long peace; whether war is innate depends on definitions.

assertions.quote: anthropologists brian ferguson and douglas frye argue that the data pinker uses is cherry-picked and inaccurate

verdicts.note: Critics show his samples skew toward violent and post-farming sites, though his defenders note that lower-violence samples have their own gaps.

assertions.quote: most agree that there has been a decline in violence over a certain period of time

verdicts.note: Homicide and per-capita war deaths fell over centuries in most datasets, though the statistical trend in war deaths is contested.
Braumoeller finds no long-term decline in the incidence or deadliness of war over 200 years, which contradicts the war part of the broad claim but does not test other kinds of violence.
Cunen et al. find interstate wars got smaller after about 1950 in the Correlates of War data, supporting a decline in war sizes only, with considerable uncertainty.
Clauset: interstate war sizes and onsets look stationary since 1823, which is consistent with a falling per-capita rate only because the population grew.
OWID: fewer conflict deaths in recent decades than in most of the 20th century, but deaths have risen again recently and the trend's future is uncertain.
